title: Personal Space Between Men
hook: Two men often stand further apart than any other pair, and the gap is rarely about dislike; it is about what closeness might be taken to mean.
why:
Watch men in a queue, at a urinal, on a sofa, in a lift. They space themselves with a precision nobody taught them: the empty seat left between two men at the cinema, the urinal skipped, the far end of the bench. Then watch the same men on a football terrace, in a rugby scrum or at a funeral, pressed together without a second thought. The rules are strict, and they change completely with the setting.

The chapter on proxemics in Part I covered the general science of personal space. This chapter is about what is specific to men with other men: why the gap is often larger, how much of it is fear of being misread, how it is changing between generations, the unwritten rules men keep, the settings that suspend those rules, how to read a change in distance between two men, and how to make room for closeness when it would help.

teach.p:
Observational studies of how people stand and sit, mostly carried out in Western countries, have often found that pairs of men keep more distance from each other than pairs of women do, with mixed pairs somewhere in between. The pattern is not universal, and it varies a great deal with culture, age, setting and relationship. But in many places, two male acquaintances talking at a party stand a little further apart, and angle themselves a little more, than two female acquaintances in the same room.

Why? Biological sex alone seems to be a poor explanation. In a 2006 study, the psychologists Uzzell and Horne measured the distances people kept and also asked about their gender roles, how strongly they identified with traditionally masculine or feminine traits. Gender role turned out to matter more than whether someone was male or female. Distance, in other words, is partly a performance of a certain kind of masculinity.

That matters for a reader. The gap between two men is rarely a measure of how much they like each other. Close friends may still stand further apart than two women who have just met. To read distance between men, compare it with what is normal for those men in that setting, not with what would be normal between other people.

The figures here stand side by side, a comfortable arm's length apart, each with his own space. Nothing in the picture says they are distant. It says they are two men in a culture where this is how two men stand.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men, in a given place, stood as close to each other as women do. In many cultures they do, and the differences found in Western studies vary with setting, which is why distance must be read against local and personal baselines.

teach.h: The fear of what closeness means.
teach.p:
The sociologist Eric Anderson coined a word for one force behind the gap: homohysteria, men's fear of being seen as gay. He argued that when that fear is high in a culture, straight men police their own behaviour and each other's, avoiding closeness, touch and tenderness between men that might be misread. When the fear falls, men have more room.

Anderson and Mark McCormack have described a shift among younger men in Britain and elsewhere. In studies of schools and sports teams, they found boys and young men hugging, leaning on each other, sharing beds on trips and expressing affection to friends in ways that, they argue, would have been unthinkable among straight boys a generation earlier. A study of older British men found many of them looking at this behaviour with disapproval, a reminder that the rules they grew up with were stricter.

This research is mostly qualitative and based on particular groups, so it should not be read as a description of all young men. But it fits what many families notice: sons who hug their friends, and fathers who keep their distance from theirs.

The fear costs everyone. It keeps straight men from comfort they might want, it makes gay men targets, and it turns ordinary closeness between friends into something to be explained or joked away. The figures here sit across a table from each other, at a careful distance. For some men, that table is not furniture but a wall.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's distance from each other showed no link to cultural attitudes to homosexuality. The evidence for the link is largely qualitative and from particular places, so it is a strong interpretation rather than a measured law.

teach.p:
Men keep a set of spacing rules that are almost never spoken aloud. At a row of urinals, a man will usually choose one that leaves a gap. At the cinema, two male friends often leave an empty seat between them. In a waiting room, men spread out to the ends of benches. In a lift, they redistribute themselves each time someone gets out.

The rules have physical effects. In a 1976 study that has become notorious, Dennis Middlemist and his colleagues measured how long it took men at a university lavatory to begin urinating when another man stood at the next urinal, one urinal away, or not at all. The closer the other man, the longer the delay, which the researchers took as evidence that crowding raises physical arousal.

The study is also taught as a warning. The men were observed in secret, through a periscope in a cubicle, without their consent and without being told afterwards. Critics called it an affront to dignity. For this book, it carries both lessons: closeness between men has measurable effects on the body, and curiosity about other people's bodies has limits that no research question overrides.

When you see a man break one of these rules, choosing the next urinal, the adjacent seat, the middle of the bench, the most likely explanation is ordinary: the place is crowded, or he did not notice, or he does not share the rule. The figures here sit together on a bench. One has taken the end; the other could have taken the other end, and chose not to. Between friends, that choice is small and warm.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's spacing in places like lavatories and cinemas were random. The pattern is widely observed, and the Middlemist study found physical effects of closeness, though it was small, old and ethically compromised.

teach.p:
The same men who keep a careful gap at a bus stop will stand pressed together on a football terrace, singing. Crowds change the rules, and the chapter on proxemics described how unwelcome crowding, on a packed commuter train, wears on the body. But a crowd you belong to is different.

In 2010 David Novelli, John Drury and Stephen Reicher tested this directly. They put people into groups and then asked them to arrange chairs for a conversation. People placed their chairs closer to someone they had been told was a member of their own group than to someone from another group, or to someone with no group label at all. Personal space, they argued, depends less on how many people are around than on who they are, and on whether we see them as us.

This explains a great deal of men's closeness. Teammates in a huddle, soldiers in a vehicle, fans on a terrace, men at a funeral, bandmates on a stage: in each case a shared identity, often marked by a shared purpose, licenses a closeness that would be uncomfortable between the same men elsewhere. The closeness often goes further: arms around shoulders, heads together, embraces after a goal.

The figures here stand shoulder to shoulder, each with an arm across the other's shoulders. It is a posture men adopt easily in a team photo and rarely on a high street. Same men, same bodies: different us.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people kept the same distance from members of their own group as from outsiders. Novelli and colleagues found that they did not, though in laboratory groups created for the study, so the size of the effect in real crowds may differ.
teach.pullQuote: Same men, same bodies: different us.

teach.h: Shoulder to shoulder, not nose to nose.
teach.p:
Men's distance depends heavily on angle. Two men who would feel uncomfortable standing half a metre apart face to face will stand shoulder to shoulder at a bar, almost touching, for an hour. On a bench, at a workbench, on a terrace or in a car, the gap between men can shrink to a few centimetres without anyone noticing.

The chapter on proxemics described how angle changes what a distance means, and the opening chapter of this part described why side by side suits so many men. Closeness side by side asks for nothing: there is no face to hold, no eye contact to manage, no question of what the closeness means. Face to face, the same distance becomes intense, whether as intimacy or as confrontation.

This has practical uses. If you want to be near a man who is struggling, sit beside him rather than in front of him. If two men are squaring up face to face, getting one of them to turn so that they stand side by side, looking at the same thing, can lower the temperature before a word is said. And if you want to talk to a man about something that matters, arrange to be shoulder to shoulder, not nose to nose.

The figures here work side by side at a bench, close enough that their elbows nearly touch. Facing each other across the same distance, they would feel the need to step back. Side by side, neither notices.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men tolerated the same distance face to face as side by side. Angle effects on comfortable distance are well established in proxemics research, though their size varies between people and cultures.

teach.p:
Because the normal gap between men is stable, changes in it are informative. When a man moves closer than usual, the rivals include warmth and trust, especially after a shared experience or a confidence; the wish to say something private; the effects of alcohol, which loosens spacing as the chapter on substance use described; and challenge. A man who closes distance face to face, chest forward, chin up, is often squaring up, which the chapter on disagreement takes up later.

When a man moves further away than usual, the rivals include discomfort with the subject, disagreement, a wish to leave, embarrassment after something has been said, and simple respect, such as giving someone room when they are upset. A friend who steps back when you put a hand on his shoulder is telling you something about that moment, not necessarily about you.

Read the change against his baseline, and alongside other channels. Distance plus a turned torso and folded arms says something different from distance plus an open stance and steady eye contact. And remember the settings that change the rules: a crowd, a team, a funeral, a bar.

The figures here show one of the plainest changes: one man leaning in, the other leaning back, turning away and folding his arms. Whatever the words between them, the bodies are negotiating distance, and the man leaning in has a choice about whether to notice.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if changes in the distance between two men carried no information about their state or relationship. Proxemics research shows that they do, but always ambiguously, which is why rivals must be considered.

teach.p:
None of this means that men should stand closer together, or that distance is a problem to be fixed. Many men are comfortable with their spacing, and the chapter on proxemics made the central rule clear: let the other person set the distance. But it is worth noticing how much closeness men deny themselves and each other out of fear of what it might mean.

Some practical steps follow. Offer closeness through a shared focus, side by side, rather than face to face. When a friend is struggling, sit beside him, and let a hand on the shoulder or a shoulder against his do some of the work, if he welcomes it. Do not police other men's closeness with jokes about what it means; those jokes are how the fear is passed on, especially to boys who are watching. If you are a father, the way you stand with your own friends teaches your son what is allowed.

Be equally careful in the other direction. Closeness that a man has not chosen, from a boss, a coach or a stranger, can be just as uncomfortable as distance, and for some men, including those with experiences of violence described in the chapter on trauma, much more so.

The figures here stand together, one with a hand resting on the other's shoulder while he bows his head. It is a small closing of the gap, offered and accepted. For many men, it is as close as they will come to another man in a year, and it may be enough.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men who wanted more closeness with other men faced no social cost for it. The research on homohysteria suggests that the cost is real but falling in some places, so how much room there is depends on where and among whom you live.

poseGallery.doCaption: Shoulder to shoulder on a bench
poseGallery.annotation: The same distance that feels like a challenge face to face feels like company side by side.
Face to face at close range raises the temperature. Turning to an angle gives both men room without anyone stepping back.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Backing away from a friend's comfort
poseGallery.annotation: A hand on the shoulder asks for nothing. If you can, let it stay a moment; if you cannot, step back gently and say so.

caseStudy:
Tom, fifty-eight, has never been a man for closeness. He shakes hands with his friends, keeps an arm's length at the pub, and once told his son Ryan, then ten, that men do not sit on each other's laps. At Tom's retirement party, Ryan, now twenty-seven, arrives with three friends who greet each other with long hugs, lean on each other at the bar and sit squashed together on a sofa. Tom feels a flicker of disapproval and then, unexpectedly, something closer to envy.

When Ryan hugs him goodbye, Tom stiffens and pats him twice on the back. Ryan notices, and lets go quickly.

A month later they go to a match together, standing on the terrace for the first time in years. In the eighty-ninth minute their team scores, and Tom finds that he has grabbed Ryan around the shoulders and is shouting into his ear. Neither of them mentions it. On the walk back to the car they are closer than they have been for years, elbows bumping.

In the pub afterwards, Tom tells Ryan about his own father, who never touched him except to shake his hand on his wedding day. Ryan listens, side by side at the bar. He does not make a joke of it.

At Christmas, when Ryan arrives, Tom hugs him first, a little awkwardly, and holds on a moment longer than a back slap would allow. Ryan's friends would not have noticed anything unusual about it. Tom notices for the rest of the day.
observe: Notice the distance men keep from each other in a queue, a waiting room or a bar, and compare it with other pairs nearby.
Notice settings where men stand much closer together, such as a team, a crowd or a funeral, and what licenses the closeness.
Notice how close you stand to male friends face to face and side by side, and whether the difference surprises you.
Notice any joke or comment that polices closeness between men, and how the men involved respond.

drills.name: Distance Map
steps: List five men you see regularly: a friend, a colleague, a relative, an acquaintance, someone you admire.
For each, estimate how far apart you usually stand or sit, face to face and side by side.
Note any settings where the distance changes, such as sport, drink or grief.
Mark any relationship where you would like the distance to be different.
Write one sentence about what the map shows you.

drills.name: Angle Experiment
steps: Next time you talk with a male friend standing face to face, notice the distance you keep.
Later in the conversation, shift so that you are side by side, looking at the same thing.
Notice whether the distance between you changes without either of you deciding it.
Afterwards, note any difference in how the conversation felt.

drills.name: The Joke That Polices
steps: Recall a time when a joke or remark made closeness between two men seem suspect or ridiculous.
Write down what was said and how the men reacted.
Write what the joke was teaching anyone who heard it, including any boys present.
Write a sentence you could say, lightly, if you hear a joke like it again.

drills.name: Read the Change
steps: Over a week, watch for moments when a man you know moves noticeably closer or further away than usual.
For each, write the rival explanations: warmth, privacy, alcohol, challenge, discomfort, disagreement, respect.
Note the other channels: torso, arms, face, voice.
Where appropriate, check your reading with a question, and record whether you were right.

quiz.q: Two old friends stand an arm's length apart while talking at a party, further apart than two women nearby who have just met. What does this chapter suggest?
options: The two men are probably not as close as they claim to be
The distance shows that they are quietly in disagreement
The gap often reflects norms for men, not how close they are
One of the men is probably uncomfortable with the other
quiz.explain: Distance between men is often larger than between women whatever the friendship, and gender roles seem to explain more of it than sex. Read distance against what is normal for those men in that setting.

quiz.q: What did Novelli, Drury and Reicher find when people arranged chairs for a conversation?
options: People placed their chairs further from members of their own group
People sat closer to someone presented as a member of their own group
The number of people in the room was the only thing that mattered
People sat closest to strangers whose group they did not know
quiz.explain: Personal space shrank when the other person was presented as one of us. Shared identity, rather than crowding as such, changed how close people were willing to be.

quiz.q: What does Eric Anderson's term homohysteria refer to?
options: Men's fear of being seen as gay, which leads them to police closeness
The anxiety that gay men feel when entering male-dominated spaces
A clinical condition involving panic in crowded public places
The excitement shared by fans when their team scores a late goal
quiz.explain: Anderson used the term for straight men's fear of being thought gay, which he argued drives avoidance of closeness, touch and tenderness between men. He and McCormack described this fear as declining among some younger men.

quiz.q: What did the 1976 lavatory study by Middlemist and colleagues find, and why is it also taught as a warning?
options: Closeness made no difference, and the study was a model of ethical care
Men urinated faster when another man stood nearby, without consent
Men refused to use urinals at all once they knew they were observed
A nearby man delayed urination, and the men were watched in secret
quiz.explain: The closer another man stood, the longer the delay before urinating, which suggests that closeness raises arousal. The men were observed through a periscope without consent or debriefing, which is why the study is used as an ethics example.

quiz.q: Two men are squaring up face to face in a pub, chests forward. You know one of them. What fits this chapter best?
options: Step between them face to face and tell them both to calm down
Get your friend to turn and stand beside you, facing the bar
Move closer to the other man so that he knows you are involved
Stay at a distance and wait to see whether anything happens
quiz.explain: Turning someone from face to face to side by side lowers the intensity of a close distance without anyone having to step back. De-escalation in depth belongs to Part VI, but changing the angle is often a good first move.

quiz.q: A friend who usually keeps his distance steps in close while telling you his marriage is in trouble. What is the best reading?
options: He is probably drunk, since he never usually stands this close
He is challenging you and wants you to step back and give way
He is uncomfortable and wants you to end the conversation now
The closeness may be trust and privacy; read it with the rest
quiz.explain: A move closer can mean warmth, privacy, alcohol or challenge. In this context, trust and the wish to speak privately are the likeliest rivals, but the other channels and his baseline should guide the reading.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific man in your life with whom you keep more distance than you would like, or less than he would like. Describe how close you usually stand or sit, in which settings the distance changes, and where you think your rules about closeness between men came from: a father, school, sport, a culture. What would one small step toward the closeness you want look like, and what would make it easier for both of you?
reflection.guidance: Be specific about the rule and where you learned it: a remark, a joke, a moment when someone pulled away from you or you pulled away from them. A small step is enough, such as sitting beside him rather than opposite, or letting a hand on the shoulder stay. If closeness from men is difficult for reasons of past harm, honour that, and do not push yourself.

failureMode: The first failure is to read the larger gap between men as coldness, when it usually reflects norms rather than feeling. The second is to ignore the force behind many of those norms, the fear of being seen as gay, and to keep passing it on through jokes and comments that boys and other men absorb. The third is to read a change in distance as one thing, warmth or challenge, without weighing the rivals and the other channels. The fourth is to impose closeness, from a position of power or on someone for whom it is unwelcome. And the fifth is to forget angle: offering closeness face to face when shoulder to shoulder would have been easy for both of you.
